title: Close Looking: Magnifiers & Lenses
strapline: The world gets bigger through the glass — legs on a woodlouse, threads in a leaf, wonders hiding in plain sight.
intent: Magnifiers hand children a scientist's superpower — the ordinary becomes extraordinary, and looking closely becomes a habit of curiosity.
Studying small things in detail sharpens observation and gives children a reason to describe precisely what they notice.
Handling lenses, focusing and steadying them on a tiny subject develops fine-motor control and patience.
Discovering the hidden detail in leaves, insects, skin, fabric and sand builds knowledge of the natural and made world and a respect for living things.
Close looking naturally sparks questions — how many legs, what are those lines, why is it furry — that lead to talk, recording and further enquiry.
It works indoors and out, alone or shared, and invites children to slow down and pay real attention.
implementation: Provide sturdy magnifiers, a bug pot or two and a tray of natural treasures — leaves, bark, feathers, shells, seeds — to examine.
Model close looking and precise wondering: 'look how many tiny lines are in this leaf — where do you think they go?'
Take magnifiers on a hunt outdoors and let children study minibeasts respectfully in place or gently in a viewer.
Offer clipboards and pencils so children can draw what they see, recording the detail the glass reveals.
Compare views — 'how does the sand look through the glass compared to without it?'
Keep interesting things to examine coming — a snail's trail, a slice of orange, a piece of your own jumper.
key_questions: Look how many tiny lines are in this leaf — where do you think they go?
How does the sand look through the glass compared to without it?
How many legs has this minibeast got?
What can you see now that you couldn't before?
Why do you think it's so furry up close?
